elements.id-string-3: \title{A variational approach to effective models for inelastic systems}\author[a]{Ghina Jezdan}\ead{Ghina.Jezdan@rub.de}\author[b]{Sanjay Govindjee}\ead{s\_g@berkeley.edu}\author[a]{Klaus Hackl}\ead{Klaus.Hackl@rub.de}\address[a]{Institute of Mechanics of Materials, Ruhr-Universit\"{a}t Bochum, D-44780Bochum, Germany}\address[b]{Structural Engineering, Mechanics, and Materials; Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, University of California, Berkeley, Berkeley CA 94720-1710, USA}
elements.id-string-5: Given a set of inelastic material models, a microstructure, a macroscopic structural geometry, and a set of boundary conditions, one can in principle always solve the governing equations to determine the system's mechanical response.
elements.id-string-6: However, for large systems this procedure can quickly become computationally overwhelming, especially in three-dimensions when the microstructure is locally complex.
elements.id-string-7: In such settings multi-scale modeling offers a route to a more efficient model by holding out the promise of a framework with fewer degrees of freedom, which at the same time faithfully represents, up to a certain scale, the behavior of the system.In this paper, we present a methodology that produces such models for inelastic systems upon the basis of a variational scheme.
elements.id-string-8: The essence of the scheme is the construction of a variational statement for the free energy as well as the dissipation potential for a coarse scale model in terms of the free energy and dissipation functions of the fine scale model.
elements.id-string-9: From the coarse scale energy and dissipation we can then generate coarse scale material models that are computationally far more efficient than either directly solving the fine scale model or by resorting to FE$^2$ type modeling.
elements.id-string-10: Moreover, the coarse scale model preserves the essential mathematical structure of the fine scale model.An essential feature for such schemes is the proper definition of the coarse scale inelastic variables.
elements.id-string-11: By way of concrete examples, we illustrate the needed steps to generate successful models via application to problems in classical plasticity, included are comparisons to direct numerical simulations of the microstructure to illustrate the accuracy of the proposed methodology.
elements.id-string-14: effective models  \sep variational inelasticity \sep micromechanics \sep inelastic homogenization \sep multiscale modeling
elements.id-string-16: Engineering systems often possess multiscale character.
elements.id-string-17: Examples are structures with internal mechanisms or elaborate design, but also complex materials with microstructure.
elements.id-string-18: To model these systems to their full extent is often not desirable considering the large computation times and problems of data storage involved, but also difficulties in interpreting the obtained results.
elements.id-string-19: Therefore, it is of high interest to devise effective models capturing the essential behavior as close as possible while relying only on a small set of essential variables.
elements.id-string-20: Focusing on microstructured materials, there are two common analysis methods seen in the literature, ones based on phenomenological models and ones incorporating direct numerical simulation (DNS).
elements.id-string-21: Phenomenological models attempt to mimic the material behaviour directly at the {macroscale}.
elements.id-string-22: While this approach leads to models which are computationally quite efficient, the observed highly complex behaviour can require the usage of a {large number of parameters}.
elements.id-string-23: Often these parameters do not have clear physical meaning and are difficult to identify.
elements.id-string-24: This makes it almost {impossible to use these models in a predictive way} because parameters identified in a specific experiment might not be suitable in a different setting.
elements.id-string-25: {DNS methods} on the other hand rely on {physically accurate theories at the microscale} using only a few parameters which are mechanistically well defined.
elements.id-string-26: While these models work efficiently at the microscale, it is possible to generate information at the macroscale only via computationally expensive procedures.
elements.id-string-27: The effort as well as the amount of data to be stored can also be so large that it becomes practically {impossible to model any sort of macroscopic system} in a meaningful way.
elements.id-string-28: Moreover, a huge quantity of information is generated at the microscale, and most of it is of no deep relevance.
elements.id-string-29: Both approaches are seen to be deficient for different reasons: either the models are efficient, but not reliable, or they are well rooted in physics and accurate, but computationally too costly.
elements.id-string-30: Both of them tend to give results which are difficult to interpret.
elements.id-string-31: In this paper we present a variational approach applied to the homogenization of inelastic materials with microstructure, that is suitable to overcome the mentioned issues.
elements.id-string-32: The approach rests on the construction of both an upscaled energy density and an upscaled dissipation potential.
elements.id-string-33: The resulting effective models possess the following features:
elements.id-string-35: they involve only parameters which are physically well-defined and measurable,the state-equations can be evaluated without resorting to elaborate computational schemes,essential material behaviour at the microscale as well as the macroscale is captured.
elements.id-string-36: The general notion of variational homogenization for inelastic systems is not entirely new.
elements.id-string-37: Models with similar properties have been derived for example for upscaling martensitic phase transformations in shape memory alloys \citep{govindjee2007upper,hackl2008micromechanical,junker2011finite,junker2014thermo,WAIMANN2016110} and  in the prediction of dislocation patterns in single crystal metals \citep{kochmann2011evolution,hackl2012zamm,gunther2015variational,Aubry20032823,ContiDolzmannKlust2009,ContiOrtiz05,miehe2010,miehe2011a,miehe2003,miehe2004}.
elements.id-string-38: More recently, an application to finite-deformation viscoelasticity has appeared in \cite{govindjee2019fully}, wherein the concept of an upscaled dissipation potential also appears within the restricted confines of the microsphere model \citep{miehe.ea:04}.

elements.id-string-502: We have presented a general variational methodology for the creation of effective or reduced models.
elements.id-string-503: The method applies to structural reductions as well as reductions to describe composite bodies.
elements.id-string-504: The central requirement is that the system's material constituents be described
elements.id-string-505: via a free energy function and a dissipation potential.
elements.id-string-506: The resulting reduced models possess a vastly reduced number of degrees of freedom, but are able to capture the essential features of the original systems.
elements.id-string-507: In contrast to typical order reduction schemes, the proposed method preserves the structure of the original system.
elements.id-string-508: In particular, our reduced models are described by a coarse grained free energy and a coarse grained dissipation function, analogous to the fine scale material's description.
elements.id-string-509: Further, the internal evolutions are governed by a coarse grained Biot principle.
elements.id-string-510: We have seen that for structural order reduction, the torsion and sphere examples, the method is quite effective and provides very good structural scale response for both perfectly plastic and linearly hardening elasoplastic materials.
elements.id-string-511: The scheme also permits recovery of fine scale fields and these are seen to be reasonable though far from perfect.
elements.id-string-512: Our methodology also proves its applicability to microstructural homogenization of elastic-perfectly plastic composites with periodic and non-periodic RVEs.
elements.id-string-514: we found good agreement concerning macroscopic stress-strain response in comparison to a detailed finite element computation.
elements.id-string-515: Unsurprisingly, we saw larger deviations when examining the predicted microscale plastic strains, just as with the structural reduction problems.
elements.id-string-516: In our opinion, this behavior was mainly caused by a strong concentration of the plastic strains in small regions in the original models, that could not be matched by the effective ones.
elements.id-string-517: Due to the coarseness, the effective models also struggle to match composite elastic stiffnesses.
elements.id-string-518: Another drawback of the proposed method is, that it is applicable only to RVEs with polygonal sub-domains, as rounded or elliptical inclusions will require the use of an infinite number of boundary normals in the procedure we have outlined.
elements.id-string-519: The use of higher order moments/variables in the definitions of the essential variables is one possible avenue of future research to resolve these last two points.
